source: This is a story about the pernicious claims borne out of a single, discredited scientific paper in 1998. But it’s also a story of how this belief has persisted among a growing number of Americans, despite its scientific foundations crumbling in the years following its origin.
why: The provided files contain New York Times article metadata and a list of studies, not survey or public-opinion data on the number of Americans holding the belief, so the growth in the number of believers cannot be computed.

source: Although chatter linking the two occasionally emerged, it was limited to a single study that found no link between autism and another, older vaccine (diptheria, whooping cough, and tetanus).
why: The files have one pre-1998 New York Times article (from 1991), but no data on studies of other, older vaccines, so the 'single study' claim cannot be checked.

source: In February of 1998, however, London doctor Andrew Wakefield publishes a study of 12 infants in a respected medical journal, The Lancet, purporting an association between autism and the mumps measles and rubella (MMR) vaccine.
why: The number of infants in Wakefield's study is not a field in the data; the CSV only contains the study's title, date, citation count and abstract, not a computable sample size.

source: A year later, the same scientific jounal publishes a study that finds no relationship between the MMR vaccine and autism among a sample of 498 children.
why: The data have no sample-size column, so the 498 children cannot be computed from the files.

source: 3 studies over the course of the next 3 years, with over 1 million children assessed, find no link between the MMR vaccine and autism.
why: The files record study dates and list membership but no numbers of children assessed, and they do not define the three-study period used here, so neither the three studies nor the million children can be reproduced.

source: In February 2004, journalist Brian Deer reveals that the Wakefield had accepted £55,000 from lawyers seeking evidence against vaccine manufacturers.
why: There is no payment or conflict-of-interest field in the data, so the £55,000 cannot be computed.

source: Of his 12 co-authors, 10 repudiated the final conclusion of their paper.
why: The data have no co-author records or repudiation information.

source: In 2006, reporting emerges that the £55K that Wakefield received from trial lawyers was actually £435,643, plus expenses.
why: There is no payment field in the data, so the £435,643 cannot be computed.

source: More reporting emerges, revealing that data for 12 of the 12 children that Wakefield included in his study was misrepresented to make vaccines appear responsible.
why: The data contain no per-child records or assessments of misrepresentation.

source: Britain experiences an outbreak of measles as a result of all the non-vaccinated children; it thereby slides behind Rwanda and Cambodia in the fight against the disease.
why: The files contain no measles case or country-ranking data.

source: 14 states struggle to contain a measles outbreak.
why: The files contain no state-level measles outbreak data, so the number of states cannot be computed.
